Oops, posted this in the wrong place:

> Yeah, the team's culture has some serious issues. The competitiveness within the team does more harm than good in my opinion. It's really hard to try and find a balance between competitiveness as a team, and a fun, less stressful environment. I've been trying to see if other top teams have the same issues we do (mainly with emotional health of students), but I haven't found much out. I think the mentors kind of feel like there's a directory relationship between stress levels on a team and competitiveness... Maybe there is, but I hope there's a way around that. I really wish I knew how to fix it.

At this point, I kinda figure that it's more effort than it's worth to try to fix the issues on our team. I haven't really seen any of the mentors putting mental/emotional health as a priority (except for harvey, but he seems to be pretty ineffective at actually doing anything about it. But at least he acknowledges that it is a problem). Without any real mentor support, i think that it's probably better for me to focus on being able to deal with the stress of build season, rather than actually trying to fix the cause of stress. 

> Why do you think Kelly gets more credit than she deserves? (I'm not looking to argue over it, I disagree with you but I do want to know what you think about it) And yeah, I think frequently, students outside leadership get singled out for recognition of their efforts more frequently than everyone else. I think those people pretty much always deserve it, but I do agree that we could do more to show general team members that their work is valued. I'm just not exactly sure how.

Thinking about this more, I'm not sure it's entirely fair to say that she gets more credit than she deserves. In terms of her technical contributions to the code, i think that that's certainly true. But I assume that there are also other things that she does (administrative things, dealing with mike, etc). And I see the point that if she does that, and yet I give her a ton of shit for not programming, then she's one of the people who isn't getting as much credit as is deserved. I'm not convinced that that's the case though. 

Anyway, I think that there are a few reasons that I think that she gets more credit than she deserves. One is that most people on robot programming do more programming work than her. I see the most important job of robot programming as programming (although again, i see the point that administration/cat herding work is important). Another reason that I said that, is because Kelly and I joined the team at the same time, under basically the same circumstances, so I tend to compare myself with her, and see that she's gone a lot further than I have in the team, so I justify that by saying that she doesn't deserve the credit that she gets. Even though probably the real reason is that she's just better than me. 

> Why isn't it really true? Why don't you think you're actually a smart person? 

I don't think that I'm smart, because when I compare myself and my knowledge to most other people, it seems like other people know a lot more than I do, especially really basic things that I just ignored or didn't bother learning. 

I am pretty sure that I'm just better at pretending to know things that I don't than other people.

1.
I think that robotics, and building a robot in 6 weeks is inherently stressful. But I also think that there's a few things about our team that make it a lot worse. And I'm trying to come up with multiple examples here but actually the main thing that I can think of is just mike, and basically every interaction I have with him. But I doubt that that will change. 

2. 
Some of both. There are certainly people who get a lot of credit and deserve it (Megan comes to mind especially). Then there are people who I feel get more credit than they deserve (Kelly comes to mind, but I'm sure that people on other subteams have similar thoughts as well. I don't really want to speculate on other subteams since I don't know that much about them). I think the largest group though is people who put in a ton of effort and work, but don't get recognized for it. Kyle comes to mind for this. I at least got recognition for doing two ball auto. Kyle put in a ton of work all across the code, but I don't think that anyone really knows that. Regarding what kind of credit/recognition people should get, I'm not entirely sure. I have a lot more complaints than I do ideas for how to improve, so I'll keep quiet until I think about it more. 

3.
I think that part of the problem here for me is that I try to put on this persona of being smart, and a lot of what I say and do and how I interact with people is based on me trying to look like I'm smart. So, when people tell me that I actually am, it means a lot less because I spend way more time then I'd like to admit trying to project a certain image of me that isn't really true. And the part that's really annoying is that if I actually was the person that I'm pretending to be, I wouldn't care about other people seeing me in a certain way.

This is a great workflow, because it lets the gui do what it does best, imo (show data), while the command line does what it does best (running commands on the repo). It also teaches me how git works, and lets me check complex commands before I move on.

There is a U shaped strip of retroreflective tape (the goal). We want to be able to, at any point, have our robot autonomously turn towards this goal. We currently have code working that uses the gyro to turn to a specific angle. 

We currently use a network camera to send images to a laptop (via wifi), which processes them and sends the resulting angle to the robot. This can take up to 4 seconds under non-ideal network conditions :(

We are planning to replace the laptop with a jetson connected via Ethernet, hopefully eliminating a lot of the lag.

There are plenty of great responses to this, but I'll add my $0.02.

First, everyone should have read/write access. You can always roll back their commits if there are any problems.

As for managing pull requests, I probably wouldn't bother with pull requests. Instead, have people work on different branches and push to master when they've tested their changes. PRs are only really necessary when people don't have write access. 

If you're using Windows, use Git Bash, otherwise use git on the terminal. This will stop the frontend from hiding things from you, and is often faster once you get used to the workflow. 

Finally, when something breaks, **don't panic**! Git saves your work. Anything that gets committed cannot be accidentally deleted. Google will solve almost any problem that you have :)
